title: Being Ambassadors for Christ at Work (1 Peter 2:9–25)
transcript: And it's lovely to be here. Thank you very much for having me this morning. Shall I just pray as we start? Heavenly Father, may the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable to you this day. Thank you that your word speaks into all aspects of our lives and has much to say about how we do our work. Please would you help us think about that well as we look at this passage this morning. Would anything I say that's true land and be really helpful to people? If I say anything wrong, would it be forgotten immediately? And we just ask all these things in your name. Amen. I thought I'd start us off this morning with a question: what do you think makes a job worthwhile? What do you think makes a job worthwhile? Is it the money? I looked it up this week, and apart from the, you know, really unusual, massively high-paid jobs like Premier League footballer, it turns out that the current top 5 most highly paid jobs in the UK are as follows: Number 1: pilots and air traffic controllers. I guess that's quite important to do right. Number 2: IT directors. Number 3: CEOs and other senior business managers. I thought it was quite striking that the IT directors get paid more. The machines are really taking over. Number 4: senior doctors, so hospital consultants. And number 5: head teachers. Maybe it's money. Maybe it's the chance to do something fun. So here are some genuine jobs that I found an advert for online this week: chocolate consultant, beer taster, Lego sculptor, or— this was my favorite— professional sleeper. I think it was something to do with research. Or maybe it's not the money, it's not the fact that it might be fun, it's the overall sense of achievement and satisfaction. A study done recently by the London School of Economics found that when you factor that in, rather than just earnings, a lot of really high-paid jobs don't actually do very well. The key things apparently that lead to job satisfaction are personal responsibility for your own work and the chance to create or build something, especially if you see it through, whereas sorting out someone else's problems or working under lots of supervision are generally less satisfying. So if you want to go for a job that has very high job satisfaction, you should consider being a painter decorator, because that comes out very high. I think those are probably the main things that our society looks for in work, aren't they? Money, fun, job satisfaction. But many of us, I imagine, feel that not all of those things, maybe none of them, are attainable. I think most of us at one time or another have felt the drudgery of work, or the way it can take over the rest of our lives more than we want it to. The Bible tells us that work is good and that God has made, created human beings to work. But like everything else, it is affected by sin. It is affected by our rebellion against God. And I think there are two particular dangers for all of us in the way we relate to our work. We can become idle, or we can make work an idol. We can become idle. We can be lazy or not approach it correctly. We can see work as a necessary evil, something that has to get done to earn money so that we can get on with what life's really about. Think of the sales manager who says, "I'm just going to fire off enough emails today so my boss doesn't think I'm slacking, get through the week, and enjoy the weekend." Or the construction worker whose attitude is, 'I'm going to do the bare minimum to pay the bills and that's job done.' But I think there's also a specifically Christian form of this that we can fall into. We can end up seeing our work as just about earning money to give to ministry or other good causes, or just as giving us a platform to evangelize. But Jesus has a lot more to say about work than that. How you actually do your actual work really matters to him as well. So that's one danger. The other danger is that we make work an idol, as in putting something else in the place of God. We can expect our work to give us a sense of identity and purpose far beyond what it is able to do. So think of the junior doctor who ruins their own health and relationships in pursuit of that dream consultant post, or the parent who is working such long hours to obtain that promotion that they never see their kids, or just the temptation that lots of us may feel to define ourselves primarily by our professional status above everything else. This morning I want us to see that if you're a Christian then no matter how you spend your working time, you have the best job in the world because you've got the best boss in the world, Jesus Christ. Have a look with me again. If you've closed your Bibles, open them up. Have a look with me again at verses 9 and 10 of our passage, which describe the amazing new status that we have if we have faith in Jesus. Peter tells his readers, you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Once you were not a people, now you are the people of God. Once you had not received mercy, now you have received Mercy. As Christians, we become part of God's people through his mercy, and that means that whoever you report to on Monday morning, Jesus is your ultimate boss. And that means that whatever you do can and should be done for his glory, or as Peter puts it, to declare his praises. And I really do mean whatever you do. I'm going to focus in most of my examples this morning on those of us in full-time paid employment outside the home, but I know I know there'll be many of you, as Sue mentioned earlier, that who have a different situation. You might be looking for work, you might be unable to work, you might be working in the home with your family, you might be retired, all kinds of other things. Whatever your situation, the basic ideas we're going to talk about this morning still apply to you. And that first principle: as God's people, Jesus is now your boss. I think really helps us avoid those two most common mistakes of either being idle or making work an idol. It stops us being idle because whatever you do has meaning and purpose. Whatever you do can be done to glorify Jesus and love your neighbor. You can be an ambassador for Jesus and his people, his nation, in your work. And it helps us stop making work an idol, because if Jesus is Lord of all of our life, he cares about us being faithful and fruitful in everything—in our work, yes, but also with our family and with our friends and with our church family and everything else. So knowing that helps us think completely differently about the supposed problem of work-life balance. Instead, we want to live as integrated, holistic people. Rather than seeing them as competing priorities or intention. And if you're not a Christian here this morning, if you're exploring Christian things, you're sort of looking into this, that is wonderful that you're here. And maybe as you listen to us sort of think about these things, it might show you that this is one way in which trusting and following Jesus is a way to live life in all its fullness. So this morning I want to unpack what it looks like to know that Jesus is your boss and to be an ambassador for him in your actual work. And I know that is difficult in practice. As you've heard, I'm not a full-time minister. I work full-time as a lawyer, so I know the pressures, and I do not have this all figured out. I know that getting the job done sometimes just squeezes out time for anything else. I know how hard it can be to get past the pleasantries and small talk and actually get to know your colleagues and be able to talk about something deeper. I know the care you sometimes have to take when you're talking about or avoiding talking about certain subjects so you don't offend somebody or get in trouble with HR. And my hope this morning is to encourage myself again and all of you that being a good witness to Jesus at work is possible. And in fact, it's a wonderful privilege. And I'm going to try and share some tips that I've picked up from other people along the way on how to go about it in a wise way. And also finally, to prepare us for the possibility of getting opposition, both theologically, so we're not surprised, our confidence isn't knocked if that happens, and also a little bit legally, because I'm a lawyer and I can't help it, to tell you your rights and how to defend yourself if that opposition comes. So let's dive in. And the first big thing I want us to see is that working for Jesus means being distinctively good. Did you see that when we read the passage? The first thing is that being a good witness to Jesus at work starts not, interestingly, with speaking about him, although as we're going to come to, that is really, really important. It starts with the distinctive way we act. So look again at verses 11 and 12. Dear friends, says Peter, I urge you as foreigners and exiles to abstain from sinful desires which wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among the pagans that though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us. The letter of 1 Peter was written to Christians in a pretty similar situation to us here today in 2025 in London. It was a small minority in a society which wasn't actively persecuting them, but which is often hostile to some aspects of the gospel and which mocks Christians sometimes or marginalizes them. And did you see that in that context, the thing that Peter first urges the Christians to do after reminding them of the status they have in Christ is to be distinctively good. Abstain from sinful desires, live good lives, do good deeds. And as we do that, those around us will notice. Even though some, he says, will accuse us of doing wrong, others, or maybe even the same people, will actually see that we're doing good, and that will glorify God. In other words, I think the Holy Spirit will use our distinctive lives to convict people of their sin and maybe bring them to faith in Christ. Have a look at verses 18 to 21 where we see the same dynamic being played out in relation to slaves and masters. So in other words, a work relationship. Peter says, slaves, in reverent fear of God, submit yourself to your masters, not only to those who are good and considerate but also to those who are harsh. For it is commendable if someone bears up under the pain of unjust suffering because they're conscious of God. How is it to your credit if you receive a beating for doing wrong and endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God. So we are to do good and we are to follow in Christ's example, even if our master is unjust or unfair. But what does that look like? Well, it's going to be very different for us in the specifics depending on our particular work. So for example, I'm a barrister, I'm involved in the legal system. My work is all about helping people resolve disputes or assisting the courts in dispensing justice. And I know God loves justice, so there are lots of ways that I have been trying to think through what it means to be distinctive in my role as I try and do that. But this is by no means something that's just for a professional job like me— mine. I have a good friend at church who is not a a barrister but a barista. He works in a coffee shop, and he tries to make really excellent coffee every day, every time, to glorify Jesus. But he also tries to think about how he can love his neighbor by being distinctively good in showing hospitality to the customers, not being the grumpy one who says, you know, here's your latte. And he's trying to go wider than that. He's tried to think through with his employer how to steward God's creation properly by suggesting some good environmentally sustainable practices. He's even asked some really good questions about ensuring that their supply chain is good and that people are treated fairly. I would urge you, it's really great to try and work out if there's a fellowship of Christians in your workplace or in your general line of work that could help you through— think through some of these specifics. So for example, um, you've got the Christian Medical Fellowship, or the Christians in Construction Network, or the Christian Police Association, Christians in the Media, The wonderfully named Glory Road Ministries for HGV drivers, Kingdom Code for software engineers, Morphe for the creative arts, and I could go on and on and on. You can check out— if you have a look, there's a website, transformworkuk.org. You can find a huge list of different areas and Christian networks in them. It's also worth checking out if there's a lunchtime talk near you. There's a website again, if you have a look at gospelatwork.org.uk, you'll find a list of them in London. And those can be a great way of popping out at lunchtime to meet other Christians other Christians working near you. You might even find someone in your own workplace you didn't know about. Or maybe explore things like the Ergon program here. It sounds a really exciting way to really go deep in the specifics of your work and how to be distinctive. I've been a member of the Lawyers Christian Fellowship for many years now, and I was— interesting— I was struck at our conference a couple of years ago that although, as expected, there were lots of particular things for lawyers, one speaker set out 4 things to think about, which I think would actually apply to any of us. So I thought I'd share them now. Here's 4 things that any of us could do to be distinctively good in our workplace. Number 1: Pursue integrity and trustworthiness. Let's be the person that when you say, "I'll get that done," you get it done. Don't cut corners. Be the person who works hard even if you're not being scrutinized and nobody might see. Obvious things: don't pad the expenses, don't get involved in anything dishonest. And this really can make a difference. A friend of ours thought for a while he was being excluded by the rest of his team at work, and he was getting worried about it. In fact, he even thought it might be some form of racial discrimination, until the Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation, and he discovered that his team had been involved in a major international bribery scandal. And they'd been keeping him out of the loop because they knew he was a Christian and they thought he wouldn't go along with it. So let's pursue integrity. Secondly, pursue love. Let's be known not just as the hard worker but as the generous one at work, the kind one, the one who listens, the one who takes an interest and takes time for people. And that might well be a sacrifice. I know there's been times that I've tried to do this and then felt really grumpy about it because it's meant I've had to stay late or do something that evening because I've taken a bit of time out of the day to try and speak to someone. But it's worth it. And on the flip side, don't be a gossip. I don't know about your workplaces, I find that probably the two key fuels for work as a lawyer are coffee and gossip. It's how people bond, it's what we all do. But we should try hard not to, because you know what? You might miss out on the news, you might think you're kind of a little bit out the loop, but people will notice. And if you stay in the same place for a few years, you might suddenly discover that people will come and talk to you when something goes wrong, or they want to ask about something, because they know they can trust you. Third thing: prayer. I should really put that one first, shouldn't I? Pray. Pray about your work. Pray for your colleagues. Pray for your clients and your customers, the ones you know, the ones that you haven't met yet. Suffuse the whole thing in prayer. And then finally, hope. This is maybe an underestimated one. Try not to be a complainer at work. I don't know about if you find this, but I find most people like a moan. I think people like a moan at work. I think also this is probably a very international crowd, but I think British people particularly like a moan. I've been in a trial in Manchester for the past 3 weeks, and every morning, without fail, the first thing that happens is I get to the court and 2 of the 4 lifts are broken, and they're also quite slow. And by the time I've got to the courtroom, the first thing I've heard is at least 3 or 4 people moaning about how slow and broken the lifts are. It's not the best way to start the morning. Let's try and be different. Let's create rather than complain. And I don't mean that means you have to be the irritating, bouncy, insensitively cheerful person that never responds well to hard things. But I do mean let's not be cynical. Let's be the can-do person, the positive person, the uplifting presence, especially when things are hard. A little while ago, I read with my kids a lovely collection of short stories by the writer Patricia St. John. And I was struck by one in particular that I thought I'd share about some missionaries to China in the late 19th century. They were apparently traveling around village markets. They were trying to sell gospels and books and giving away tracts and speaking of Jesus. And they were getting a bit down at the lack of interest when one little man piped up and he said, 'Oh, I know the man you're talking about. I've met him.' And they said, 'No, no, I think you've misunderstood. Jesus left this earth 1900 years ago. You can't possibly have met him in person. But the man insisted. He said, I've, I've met that man, and he offers to take them to the next village to meet him. Obviously, the missionaries are completely confused by this, but they're not going to pass up the opportunity, so they trundle along to the next village. And when they get there, it's a pretty poor village. It is uncared for. It's in a sad state. But there is one little house that is different. There's no rubbish. The garden is tended. And their guide introduces them to the owner, who greets them politely, and they go in. And they tell him that they're selling books. What about? Oh, God the Creator and his Son Jesus. And the man's face lights up. Jesus, how wonderful! Do you know him too? Is he the same man I know? And he goes into the back and gets this box and comes out with an old tattered copy of the Gospel of Mark. And he says, years ago I bought this in the market and I read it from COVID to cover. I've never known anyone like this. He's so good. I wanted to be like him, so I've just been trying to do that every single day. I ask myself, how can I follow him? Do you know him too? That is what we want to be like in our workplaces. We want to be the person who, when others see how we act, they think, that looks a bit like Jesus.. But one final thought on this. If you've just been listening to all of that and you've been thinking, well, that sounds great, but I am a total failure, I just think back in the last week and I have totally screwed up and haven't even begun to do any of that, well, join the club. And that's why verses 24 and 25 of this passage are so encouraging. Peter reminds us that Jesus has borne our sins. So we can pick ourselves up and we can try again. Let's try again tomorrow. Monday morning, you can go in there knowing that your failures are forgiven and you can try and be distinctively good once again. So that's the big thing we see first. But then secondly, being distinctive should lead to people noticing. And that means we need to be ready to speak of Jesus. How does that work? Well, we see in verse 12— we saw, didn't we, that people will glorify God on the day he visits us? It's maybe not quite clear there how exactly that works. I think if we actually look over to the next chapter, if you look over the page, Peter unpacks it a little bit. In chapter 3, verse 15, he says this: In your hearts, revere Christ as Lord. 'Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who speak maliciously against your good behavior in Christ may be ashamed of their slander.' So I think this is how it works. Peter expects us to live distinctive lives, including our workplaces. People will notice that, and then they'll ask us questions. They'll ask us, 'Why are you different?' or they'll want to be friends or confide in us because we're not the gossip. And that will give us opportunities to speak of our hope in Jesus. So we need to expect that, we need to prepare for that, and we need to pray for that to happen. And I don't think that means we need to go on any special apologetics course or a how-to-answer-the-top-5-hardest-questions-about-Christianity primer. It is wonderful to do those things, You should think deeply about the Christian worldview and what it has to say about the issues of the day, but that's just because it's really good to do in and of itself. It's not just as a means to answer questions smartly, because our answers, I think, should be personal, real, the overflow of our ongoing relationship with God and our developing discipleship in the way of Jesus, warts and all. And did you see as well How Peter emphasizes we should speak. In verses 15 and 16, he says, doesn't he, with supreme eloquence and great emotion? No, no, he doesn't say that. With every perfect answer? No, he doesn't say that. He says with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience. It is vitally important that we witness to Jesus in how we speak of him, not just what we say. And if we do it in the way that Peter wants, we will not only be more persuasive, I think, but also less likely to face bad consequences. Because he says, verse 16, if somebody objects and is opposing us, they will see that that opposition is unfair and be put to shame for slandering us. I'd love to commend to you an excellent resource produced by the Evangelical Alliance. It's called Living for Jesus at Work. There you go, it's up on the screen, and there's a link there if you want to get it. That contains some great advice on how to speak of Jesus well in the workplace. A good way to remember the main ideas is these four words: pray, care, ask, share. Pray, care, ask, share. We've kind of dealt with the first two already, right? Pray. Pray about it all in advance. Pray for your colleagues. Care. Be the person who actually cares about them. But then ask and share. So ask when there's an opportunity to share your Christian faith with someone. Ask questions as well as just telling them what you think. The more you take a genuine interest in their life, the more they want to hear about yours. And then share. Share in a personal way. Explain the impact the Christian faith has on your life and your day-to-day work. And did you know, as a matter of law, if you express an opinion rooted in your Christian beliefs, you have much greater legal protection than if you just express your opinion on a topic at all. So for that reason, you really want to be open about the fact that the gospel impacts on how you think about things, or that Jesus tells you to think differently. It actually gives you much more protection. The other important point that that resource makes, and then thinks through the practical implications of it— and this is in line with 1 Peter— is know when to stop. Make sure that you show to others and their faith the same respect you would want to be afforded to yours, because we want workplaces where everybody has freedom to live out their faith. If you speak to a colleague about their faith, or a customer or client, check they're happy to do it and to continue with it. And if you're in a position of authority in particular, be sensitive to that. Don't abuse your power. If somebody makes it clear they don't want to talk about anymore, then you can leave it. It's up to the Holy Spirit what happens with the words you've shared. There was a case a few years ago of a nurse who got disciplined for sharing the gospel at work, and it seemed like that was a terrible infringement of her freedom. And then the kind of facts came out in detail, and it turned out what had happened is she had repeatedly pestered a young junior Muslim colleague who she was managing to come along to a Christian event when they'd made clear they didn't really want to come. And actually, I think it was right that she was disciplined for that. Peter says, what credit is it to you if you get punished for doing something wrong? So let's be distinctive in our work. Let's be ready then to speak of Jesus when we get opportunity and we are asked questions. And then thirdly and finally, let's be ready for the fact that people will not always like that, but God will be glorified. Because you see, the thing is, even if you follow all those tips, you are still probably going to expect some opposition sometimes. Even if you're a model employee, there may be some pressure for speaking and living for Jesus. After all, even Jesus himself, who spoke and lived of God perfectly, was opposed to the point of death. And did you see in our passage Peter takes that for granted? Back in verse 12, if you look back to that, he says, 'Though they accuse you of doing wrong.' He assumes it will happen. Or in verse 18, he assumes that some of us will have unjust masters. Christians being made fun of and unfairly accused of being judgmental or narrow-minded or all sorts of other things is nothing new. In the Roman world that Peter's writing into, there were vicious rumors that circulated that Christians were rebellious because they didn't acknowledge that Caesar was God, even though they did honor him. There were rumors that they were undermining the manly Roman virtues because the church was really popular with women and with slaves, and so on and so on. So we should expect to be slandered. And we should expect to, to feel uncomfortable at times and to have situations where our conscience as Christians might come into conflict with the demands of the workplace. We might be pressured to do something dishonest or deceitful. It might be because what we believe comes into conflict with the views of others, and we're willing to be tolerant and even love them, but they're not. They're not willing to live and let live. That shouldn't be a surprise. As Peter says in verse 11, we are foreigners and exiles. Christians are strangers in this world. Our true home is the new creation. And there are wonderful examples throughout the Bible of people who have taken a stand faithfully when the pressure comes on. I'm sure you can think of loads of them. One of my favorite is Daniel and his friends at the beginning of Daniel. Do you remember that story when they are being indoctrinated into Babylonian culture, him and his fellow students, and they pursue excellence? They're trying to be as good as they possibly can be, and they go along with a lot of the assimilation, but they do draw a line somewhere. They don't take food from the king's table. And I think we can, we can learn some basic principles from that. We might have to pick our battles. We can maybe go along with some things and take a stand somewhere. And I think that's okay as long as you've thought it through and you've prayed about it and carefully decided in good conscience. We might reach different conclusions, but we will probably have to take a stand somewhere, and we should probably try to do it early so we're ready to take a stand on something bigger if it comes up. Obviously, we're in a much better position than Daniel and his friends. We don't live in an absolute totalitarian monarchy. We live in a liberal democracy here in the UK with strong protections for religious freedom and against religious discrimination in workplace. Again, that Evangelical Alliance booklet has some great explanations of this and of the protections you have in law against being discriminated against because of your beliefs. But it can still get tricky on individual issues. I thought just as we close, I'd give one example just to show how we might work it through. And I'm sure you can think of many others. Um, what would you do, for example, if, um, your workplace now required you to include your preferred pronouns in your email signature or introduce yourself with them at a meeting? Now, I personally wouldn't do that, but Christians could come to different conclusions about it. I think as long as, I said, you've thought about it, you've prayed about it, talked about it with other Christians, and your conscience is clear, you might decide different ways. But let's just think it through. That idea, that instruction from your employer, is probably born out of a good desire to be inclusive to trans people, and also maybe to help with cross-cultural communication, because maybe if you're not familiar with the culture's names, you might not know if somebody's male or female on the end of an email. And as long as you do that with gentleness and respect, and you treat any of your actual colleagues with real love and dignity, it is likely the law would protect you if your manager tried to compel you against your conscience. Belief in the importance of biological sex as opposed to gender identity is protected in law here in the UK. The Equality Act 2010, as the Supreme Court recently confirmed—you might have seen that in the news—says that sex means biological sex. Now that's just one example. There may well be all kinds of other situations that will come up A lot of them are dealt with in that great resource, Living for Jesus at Work. But I just wanted to kind of give one way that the pressure might come on and how to think about responding to it. But let's draw things to a close. We have the enormous privilege of working for the best boss in the world, Jesus Christ. Knowing that helps us avoid those twin traps of being idle or making work an idol. Instead, we can be an ambassador for him at work. So let's honor him. Let's behave distinctively well in the workplace. Let's pray that that gives us opportunities to speak of him and answer people when they ask why are we being different. Don't be surprised if that's not always popular, or we have to wrestle through some difficult conflicts. But take heart that God will be glorified. Shall I pray? Heavenly Father, thank you so much that your word speaks into all aspects of our lives, and including what we do in our work. Thank you that we are now your people and we're ambassadors for you, for the privilege of doing that. And we pray, Father, that you would help us live differently, live distinctively well, be distinctively good in our work, that you would then give us, Father, opportunities to speak of you. Please, even this week, would you be giving us chances to say something of Jesus? And please, Father, if the pressure comes on and we face opposition, would we not be surprised? Would we respond with gentleness, with respect, reasonably? And we would be prepared to honor you and see you glorified, whatever the outcome.
